title: contoso 2.3.0
text:
read_reports() returns 118 fictional internal business reports about Contoso’s 2025 trading (weekly sales flashes, monthly e-commerce, supply chain and plant reviews, quarterly regional reviews, pricing committee minutes, operations notices, industry notes and the Annual Operating Plan). The figures come from the “mega” cloud dataset. Some reports carry deliberate errors, for testing financial planning and analysis assistants. The reports ship compressed in inst/extdata/reports.rds (about 90 KB).
export_reports() writes the reports as one YAML file each, the layout document stores and retrieval tools expect. This adds ‘yaml12’ to Imports.
New vignette, vignette("business-reports"), describing the reports. New articles on the website: “Getting started” and “Searching the reports with ragnar”.





Removed contoso_dict_columns(). The data dictionary is a standard data-dict file, so the data-dict CLI already reads, validates and renders it, and yaml::read_yaml() reads it in R. Use system.file("extdata", "small", "data-dict.yaml", package = "contoso") to find it.





yaml has moved from Imports to Suggests; it was only needed by the function removed above.
Depends is now R (>= 4.1.0), which the package code has in fact required for some time – it uses the native pipe |> and the \(x) function shorthand.





Fixed size = "large", where every row of fx was present twice (200,900 rows over 100,450 distinct rates, exact duplicates). Joining sales to fx doubled the row count and any revenue converted through it. medium and mega were unaffected, and contoso_10m/fx.parquet is now byte-identical to the file the other sizes already shared. This is the same duplication fixed for sales in 2.2.0; fx was missed at the time.





The bundled data dictionary now validates against the data-dict spec at all three levels (validate-spec, validate-meta, validate-data). Removed the non-spec rows and missing keys, added the required range to every ordered column, and recorded the composite primary keys on sales and orderrows (order_key + line_number) and on fx (date + from_currency + to_currency).
Corrected the dictionary where it contradicted the data: line_number is zero-based, not 1-based, and the sales-to-fx join was documented as many-to-one when it fans out five-to-one unless from_currency is filtered.
The derived measures in sales are now written as checkable assertions rather than prose, so data-dict validate-data verifies that gross_revenue, net_revenue, unit_discount, discounts, cogs, gross_margin and unit_margin still follow their documented formulas.
The dictionary for the cloud datasets ships as inst/extdata/cloud/data-dict.yaml, covering size = "medium", "large" and "mega". It carries the same types, constraints, assertions, relationships and glossary as the small dictionary; only the observed range, examples and the descriptions that are genuinely different differ.
The reports returned by read_reports() have their own data dictionary, inst/extdata/reports/data-dict.yaml, describing each column and noting that some reports are deliberately wrong.

title: contoso 2.3.0
text:
Breaking changes

customer now has one row per customer (3,165 rows, down from 7,794). Previous versions built it by joining the customer catalogue onto sales, which repeated each customer once per sales line they appeared on. This made customer_key non-unique, so joining customer to sales, orders or any other table silently multiplied rows. No attribute varied within a customer, so the deduplication loses no data, but any code that relied on the old row count — or that worked around the fan-out with distinct() — should be reviewed. Thanks to Hadley Wickham for reporting.
The cloud dataset behind create_contoso_duckdb(size = "small") carried the same fan-out and has been corrected, so it again matches the bundled customer. The medium, large and mega sizes were never affected.

title: contoso 2.3.0
text:
Cloud dataset fixes

Column types are now consistent across all four sizes. Previously date columns were stored as strings in medium and large — so comparisons on order_date and friends were string comparisons, and date arithmetic failed — while small and mega used real dates. Integer widths also varied (DOUBLE, INTEGER, BIGINT) between sizes, and in medium sales.order_date was a date while orders.order_date was a string. Dates are now DATE, keys and counts BIGINT, and measures DOUBLE, everywhere.
Fixed size = "large", where every row of sales was present twice (47,439,870 rows over 23,719,935 order lines, exact duplicates). Any revenue, cost, margin or quantity total taken from that size was doubled. The documented row count for large was the inflated figure and is now 23,719,935. Other sizes were unaffected.
Fixed product_code in medium and large, which was stored as an integer and had lost its leading zero (101001 rather than 0101001), so it did not match the same product’s code in small and mega.

title: The business reports
text:
contoso includes 118 fictional internal business reports about Contoso’s 2025 trading. They are the documents a finance team reads alongside its sales data: weekly flashes, monthly reviews, quarterly country reports, committee minutes and plan memos. Each is written by a named person in a named business unit, published on a realistic date, and based on the “mega” dataset from create_contoso_duckdb("mega").

title: The business reports
text:
A sample report
The Weekly Sales Flash for week 20, in full:

sample <- dplyr::filter(reports, id == "sales-flash-2025-w20")
cat(sample$body)
#> # Weekly Sales Flash - Week 20 (12 May 2025 to 18 May 2025)
#> Priya Raman, Director of Sales Operations, Sales Operations | 19 May 2025
#> 
#> **Headline**
#> - Net revenue **$590M**, flat on Wk 19 (-0.6%) and **down 9% YoY**. Third clean week since stocktake ended, so the run-rate is settling at about $590M a week.
#> - Stores **up 2.5% YoY** (+0.3% WoW). Online is still the whole problem at **down 17% YoY**.
#> - GM steady at **56.0%** and discount at 5.9%, so we are not buying volume.
#> 
#> | | Wk 20 | WoW | YoY |
#> |---|---|---|---|
#> | Net revenue | $590M | -0.6% | -9.3% |
#> | Online | $334M | -1.2% | -16.6% |
#> | Stores | $257M | +0.3% | +2.5% |
#> | GM % | 56.0% | | |
#> | Discount % | 5.9% | | |
#> | Units | 2.39M | | |
#> 
#> **Channel**
#> - **Online:** The marketplace hole hasn't closed. Migration to contoso.com is still well below what the AOP assumed, and the lower paid-search spend isn't helping. Online is down another 1.2% WoW.
#> - **Stores:** Holding up, and the gains come from the Store Next countries.
#> 
#> **Country**
#> - **Wave 1 countries are strong:** Italy +28% YoY, Netherlands +27%, Germany +25% and France +11%. All four were up WoW except Italy, which was -1%.
#> - **Wave 2:** Canada +13% YoY, +1% WoW. Australia +9% YoY but **-4.7% WoW**, the weakest country this week.
#> - **UK:** +3% YoY and +2.7% WoW as conversions start.
#> - **US:** -11% YoY and -0.5% WoW. There are no converted stores until the July pilot.
#> 
#> **Category**
#> - **Cameras:** +28% YoY. The A. Datum creator line and the experience zones are still working.
#> - **Audio** +23% and **Games and Toys** +16%. Both are getting the freed-up floor space.
#> - **TV and Video:** **-36% YoY** and -4.3% WoW, which is far deeper than the ~8% decline the range reset planned for.
#> - **Home Appliances:** -17% YoY. The Litware stop-sell is still leaving gaps on the microwave and coffee-machine shelves.
#> - **Computers:** -10% YoY at $209M. We should be in the peak of the Win10 refresh, and it isn't showing up.
#> - **Cell phones:** Flat, -2% YoY.
#> 
#> **Watch list**
#> - **Run-rate vs plan:** ~$590M/week annualises to roughly $31B against the $35B AOP. H2 has to do more work.
#> - **Computers:** If the refresh isn't landing in H1, find out where the demand went.
#> - **TV and Video:** Check whether the decline is still sliding WoW or has found a floor.
#> - **Australia:** Check whether the WoW dip is a one-off or a sign that the wave 2 benefit is fading.
#> - **UK:** Track the converted-store lift as the May to July wave rolls out.

title: The business reports
text:
The year in the reports
Reports run from the plan memo in December 2024 to the last reviews of 2025, published in January 2026:

reports |>
  dplyr::count(month = format(published, "%Y-%m"), name = "reports")
#> # A tibble: 14 × 2
#>    month   reports
#>    <chr>     <int>

#>  2 2025-01       6
#>  3 2025-02       7
#>  4 2025-03      10
#>  5 2025-04      13
#>  6 2025-05       7
#>  7 2025-06       8
#>  8 2025-07      14

#> 10 2025-09       9
#> 11 2025-10      12
#> 12 2025-11       8
#> 13 2025-12       8
#> 14 2026-01       8

Together they tell one story about 2025: an exit from third-party marketplaces, a TV range reset, a store refit programme (“Store Next”), a product recall, a PC refresh, and the usual stocktake, summer shutdown and holiday season. Each author only knows what their unit would know on the publication date.
Some reports are deliberately wrong. A few authors misread the data or credit the wrong cause, as real business writing does. The package does not say which, so an FP&A assistant has to find them by checking the reports against the data.

title: Sales Data from the Contoso Dataset
text:
Source: R/data.R
This dataset contains information about sales orders, including order details, pricing, and customer data from the Contoso dataset. It provides insights into the transactions that have occurred, including order dates, delivery dates, customer and store information, as well as product details.

title: Sales Data from the Contoso Dataset
text:
Usage
sales

title: Sales Data from the Contoso Dataset
text:
Details

Each row is one line item on one order — the same grain as orderrows. This is the denormalised fact table: it repeats every column of orders and orderrows, adds the day’s exchange_rate, and pre-computes seven revenue, cost and margin measures.

title: Sales Data from the Contoso Dataset
text:
Format

A data frame with 7,794 rows and 20 columns:



order_key



double Unique identifier for each order.



line_number



double Line number within the order (for multi-line orders).



order_date



Date Date when the order was placed.



delivery_date



Date Date when the order was delivered.



customer_key



double Unique identifier for the customer who placed the order.



store_key



double Unique identifier for the store where the order was placed.



product_key



double Unique identifier for the product in the order.



quantity



double The quantity of the product ordered.



unit_price



double The price per unit of the product.



net_price



double The price per unit after discount, in USD. Despite the name this is a unit figure, not a line total.



unit_cost



double The cost per unit of the product.



currency_code



character The currency the order was placed in (e.g., USD, EUR). Does not describe the money columns, which are all USD.



exchange_rate



double The USD-to-currency_code rate on order_date, from fx. 1.0 for USD orders. It has not been applied to the money columns — multiply if you want local currency.



gross_revenue



double A product’s unit_price multiplied by quantity.



net_revenue



double A product’s net_price multiplied by quantity.



unit_discount



double A product’s unit_price minus net_price.



discounts



double A product’s unit_discount multiplied by quantity.



cogs



double Cost of goods sold. A product’s unit_cost multiplied by quantity.



gross_margin



double A product’s net_revenue minus cogs.



unit_margin



double A product’s gross_margin divided by quantity.

title: Sales Data from the Contoso Dataset
text:
Currency

Every money column is in USD, regardless of the order’s currency_code, so amounts sum directly across orders. Multiply by exchange_rate to express an amount in the currency the order was placed in.

https://github.com/sql-bi/Contoso-Data-Generator-V2-Data/releases/tag/ready-to-use-data

title: Product Data from the Contoso Dataset
text:
Source: R/data.R
This dataset contains information about products in the Contoso dataset. It includes product details such as identifiers, descriptions, pricing, weight, and categorization. This dataset is useful for analyzing product characteristics, pricing, and product-related sales insights.

title: Product Data from the Contoso Dataset
text:
Usage
product

title: Product Data from the Contoso Dataset
text:
Format

A data frame with 2,517 rows and 14 columns:



product_key



double Unique identifier for each product.



product_code



character A code that uniquely identifies the product.



product_name



character The name or description of the product.



manufacturer



character The name of the manufacturer of the product.



brand



character The brand of the product.



color



character The color of the product.



weight_unit



character The unit weight is expressed in: “grams”, “ounces” or “pounds” — never “kg”. Metric and imperial units are mixed, so weight is not comparable across rows without converting. Missing where the product has no weight.



weight



double The weight of the product, in weight_unit. Not on a common scale — see that column.



cost



double The cost price of the product.



price



double The selling price of the product.



category_key



double Unique identifier for the category to which the product belongs.



category_name



character The name of the category to which the product belongs.



sub_category_key



double Unique identifier for the subcategory to which the product belongs.



sub_category_name



character The name of the subcategory to which the product belongs.

Writes each report from read_reports() as a YAML file named ⁠<id>.yaml⁠, holding the metadata fields and the Markdown text in body. yaml12::read_yaml() reads a file back in one call.

text:
Usage
export_reports(dir, overwrite = FALSE)

title: Write the Contoso business reports to files
text:
Arguments


dir



Directory to write to. Created if it does not exist.



overwrite



Replace files that already exist?

title: Write the Contoso business reports to files
text:
Value

The paths of the written files, invisibly.

title: Write the Contoso business reports to files
text:
Examples

dir <- file.path(tempdir(), "contoso-reports")
paths <- export_reports(dir)

title: Creates DuckDB database with Contoso datasets
text:
Source: R/database.R
Creates a DuckDB connection with Contoso datasets loaded from cloud storage. The datasets are stored as Parquet files on Cloudflare R2 and streamed directly into DuckDB.

title: Creates DuckDB database with Contoso datasets
text:
Usage
create_contoso_duckdb(size = "small")

title: Creates DuckDB database with Contoso datasets
text:
Arguments


size



Dataset size: “small”, “medium”, “large”, or “mega”

title: Creates DuckDB database with Contoso datasets
text:
Value

A list containing:




sales, product, customer, store, fx, calendar, orders, orderrows: lazy tbl objects




con: the DuckDB connection (use DBI::dbDisconnect(db$con, shutdown = TRUE) when done)

title: Creates DuckDB database with Contoso datasets
text:
Details

The create_contoso_duckdb() function creates views for the following Contoso datasets:




sales: Contains sales transaction data.




product: Contains details about products, including attributes like product name, manufacturer, and category.




customer: Contains customer demographic and geographic information.




store: Contains information about store locations and attributes.




fx: Contains foreign exchange rate data for currency conversion.




calendar: Contains various date-related information, including day, week, month, and year.




orders: Contains order header information.




orderrows: Contains order line items.




Available sizes (sales rows):




small: 7,794




medium: 2,349,091




large: 23,719,935




mega: 237,245,485

title: Creates DuckDB database with Contoso datasets
text:
Schemas

Column names, order and types are identical across all four sizes: date columns are DATE, keys and counts are BIGINT, and measures are DOUBLE. Only the row counts differ.


size = “small” serves the same data as the bundled sales, customer and friends. The larger sizes come from separate generator runs, so they cover a different date range and a much larger customer catalogue – including customers who never place an order, which the bundled data excludes.

title: Creates DuckDB database with Contoso datasets
text:
Examples

  db <- create_contoso_duckdb(size = "small")
  db$sales |> head()
  DBI::dbDisconnect(db$con, shutdown = TRUE)

title: contoso
text:
Source Code
Report a Bug




MIT + file LICENSE



Citing this package




Alejandro Hagan (author, maintainer)
Contoso is a synthetic dataset containing sample sales transaction data for the fictional “Contoso” company. It includes various supporting tables for business intelligence, such as customer, store, product, and currency exchange data.
This dataset is perfect for practicing time series analysis, joins, financial modeling, or any business intelligence-related tasks.
It comes with a built-in dataset as well as the ability to create an in-memory database with duckdb
The package comes with the following tables:
Built into the package is the smallest version of the dataset: 7,794 sales lines across 3,242 orders and 3,165 customers.
Every column is documented in a machine-readable data-dict dictionary, shipped with the package. There is one per dataset, each in its own directory: extdata/small/ describes the bundled tables (and size = "small"), extdata/cloud/ describes the medium, large and mega sizes.
Both validate against the spec, so the data-dict CLI can check either against its data, or render it as a browsable page. Point it at the directory:
Using labelled::look_for(), you can also see the columns’ labels from the labelled package.
For larger datasets, use create_contoso_duckdb() with one of the following sizes:
Column names and types are identical across all four sizes; only the row counts differ.

Installation
You can install the package from CRAN:
install.packages("contoso")
Or install the development version from Codeberg:
# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_git("https://codeberg.org/usrbinr/contoso")


Example
library(contoso)

# Create a DuckDB connection to Contoso datasets
db <- create_contoso_duckdb(size = "medium")

# Access the sales dataset
db$sales |> head()

# Launch the DuckDB UI to explore all tables interactively
launch_ui(db$con)

# Clean up when done
DBI::dbDisconnect(db$con, shutdown = TRUE)


Business reports
The package also ships 118 fictional internal business reports about Contoso’s 2025 trading: weekly sales flashes, monthly e-commerce, supply chain and plant reviews, quarterly regional reviews, pricing committee minutes, operations notices, industry notes and the Annual Operating Plan. Their figures come from the “mega” dataset, and a few contain deliberate errors, for testing document search and FP&A assistants.
reports <- read_reports()            # one row per report, Markdown text in `body`
export_reports("contoso-reports")    # or write them as one YAML file each
See the “Business reports” and “Searching the reports with ragnar” articles on the package website.

title: Calendar Dimension Data from the Contoso Dataset
text:
Source: R/data.R
This dataset contains calendar-related information used for time-based analysis in the Contoso dataset. It includes various representations of date-related attributes, such as year, quarter, month, and day, along with indicators for working days. It is useful for time-series analysis and aggregating data by different time periods.

title: Calendar Dimension Data from the Contoso Dataset
text:
Usage
calendar

title: Calendar Dimension Data from the Contoso Dataset
text:
Details

Spans whole calendar years, so it extends past the trading period at both ends. Join from calendar when you need a dense series with explicit zeros.

title: Calendar Dimension Data from the Contoso Dataset
text:
Format

A data frame with 1,461 rows and 17 columns:



date



Date The actual date for the record.



date_key



double The date as YYYYMMDD.



year



double The year part of the date.



year_quarter



character Quarter and year, formatted “Q1-2021”.



year_quarter_number



double A continuous quarter counter, year * 4 + quarter, running from 8085. Not 1-4 — use quarter for the within-year number.



quarter



character The quarter within the year (e.g., “Q1”, “Q2”).



year_month



character Month and year, formatted “January 2021”.



year_month_short



character Month and year, formatted “Jan 2021”.



year_month_number



double A continuous month counter, year * 12 + month, running from 24253. Not YYYYMM.



month



character The month name (e.g., “March”).



month_short



character The abbreviated month name (e.g., “Mar”).



month_number



double The month within the year, 1-12.



day_of_week



character The full name of the day of the week (e.g., “Monday”).



day_of_week_short



character The abbreviated day of the week (e.g., “Mon”).



day_of_week_number



double The day within the week, starting Sunday = 1, not Monday.



working_day



double Indicator of whether the date is a working day (1 for working day, 0 for non-working day). This is the flag.



working_day_number



double A cumulative count of working days elapsed, running 0-1003. Not a flag: it increments on working days and repeats on non-working days.

title: Customer Data from the Contoso Dataset
text:
Changed in 2.2.0

Up to version 2.1.0 this table was built by joining the customer catalogue onto sales, which repeated each customer once per sales line they appeared on: 7,794 rows for 3,165 customers. customer_key was therefore not unique and any join to this table silently multiplied rows. The duplicates have been collapsed. No attribute varied within a customer, so nothing was lost.

title: Launch the DuckDB UI in your browser
text:
Source: R/database.R
The launch_ui() function installs and launches the DuckDB UI extension for an active DuckDB database connection. This allows users to interact with the database via a web-based graphical interface.
Your connection from create_contoso_duckdb() is returned in the list.

title: Launch the DuckDB UI in your browser
text:
Usage
launch_ui(.con)

title: Launch the DuckDB UI in your browser
text:
Arguments


.con



A valid DBIConnection object connected to a DuckDB database. The function will check that the connection is valid before proceeding.

title: Launch the DuckDB UI in your browser
text:
Value

The function is called for its side effects and does not return a value. It launches the DuckDB UI and opens it in your default web browser.

title: Launch the DuckDB UI in your browser
text:
Details

The function performs the following steps:




Checks that the provided DuckDB connection is valid. If the connection is invalid, it aborts with a descriptive error message.




Installs the ui extension into the connected DuckDB instance.




Calls the start_ui() procedure to launch the DuckDB UI in your browser.




This provides a convenient way to explore and manage DuckDB databases interactively without needing to leave the R environment.

title: Launch the DuckDB UI in your browser
text:
See Also



create_contoso_duckdb() for creating example Contoso datasets in DuckDB.




DBI::dbConnect() and DBI::dbDisconnect() for managing DuckDB connections.




duckdb::duckdb() for creating a DuckDB driver instance.

title: Launch the DuckDB UI in your browser
text:
Examples

# Connect to DuckDB
db <- create_contoso_duckdb()

# Launch the DuckDB UI
launch_ui(db$con)

# Clean up
DBI::dbDisconnect(db$con, shutdown = TRUE)

title: Store Data from the Contoso Dataset
Store Data from the Contoso Dataset
text:
The online channel

store_key 999999 is the online channel, not a location. It carries sentinel values throughout: store_code and geo_area_key are -1, country_code is “–”, country_name and state are literally “Online”, and square_meters is missing. Filter it out before any geographic or floor-space aggregate. It accounts for a little over half of all sales lines.

title: Getting started
text: contoso gives you the same retail dataset in two ways: as tables bundled with the package, and as larger cloud versions you query through ‘DuckDB’.

title: Getting started
Getting started
text:
Larger datasets in ‘DuckDB’
create_contoso_duckdb() streams the Parquet files from cloud storage into an in-memory ‘DuckDB’ database. Pick a size by the number of sales rows:



size
sales rows




"small"
7,794


"medium"
2,349,091


"large"
23,719,935


"mega"
237,245,485



"small" is the same data as the bundled tables. The other sizes cover a different date range and a much larger customer catalogue.

db <- create_contoso_duckdb(size = "medium")

The result is a list with one lazy table per dataset and the connection, db$con. Write dplyr as usual; it runs in ‘DuckDB’ until you collect():

db$sales |>
  dplyr::summarise(net_revenue = sum(net_revenue), .by = currency_code) |>
  dplyr::collect()

Use launch_ui() to browse every table in the ‘DuckDB’ UI, and disconnect when you are done:

launch_ui(db$con)

DBI::dbDisconnect(db$con, shutdown = TRUE)

title: Getting started
text:
Data dictionary
Every table and column is described in a data-dict file, with keys, joins and the formulas behind each measure:

system.file("extdata", "small", "data-dict.yaml", package = "contoso")

Use "cloud" in place of "small" for the dictionary of the larger sizes.

title: Getting started
text:
Next steps
The package also includes 118 fictional business reports about Contoso’s 2025 trading. See The business reports to read them, and Searching the reports with ragnar to search them.

title: Searching the reports with ragnar
text:
This article loads the business reports into a ragnar store: a single ‘DuckDB’ file you can search by keyword, filter by report metadata, query with SQL, and hand to an LLM as context.
The store uses BM25 keyword search only. There are no embeddings, so you need no embedding model, provider or API key to build or search it.
The one design rule: every chunk carries all of its report’s metadata as typed columns. That is what lets you filter by publication date, unit or report type inside the database, and cite the source of every hit.
You need these packages:

install.packages(c("ragnar", "dplyr", "purrr", "DBI"))

title: Searching the reports with ragnar
text:
This article loads the business reports into a ragnar store: a single ‘DuckDB’ file you can search by keyword, filter by report metadata, query with SQL, and hand to an LLM as context.
The store uses BM25 keyword search only. There are no embeddings, so you need no embedding model, provider or API key to build or search it.
The one design rule: every chunk carries all of its report’s metadata as typed columns. That is what lets you filter by publication date, unit or report type inside the database, and cite the source of every hit.
You need these packages:

install.packages(c("ragnar", "dplyr", "purrr", "DBI"))

title: Searching the reports with ragnar
text:
Step 1: read the reports
read_reports() returns one row per report: eight metadata columns (the dates already as Date) and a body column with the Markdown text.

reports <- read_reports()


dplyr::glimpse(reports |> select(-body))
#> Rows: 118
#> Columns: 8
#> $ id           <chr> "aop-2025", "sales-flash-2025-w01", "sales-flash-2025-w02…
#> $ title        <chr> "2025 Annual Operating Plan - Summary", "Weekly Sales Fla…
#> $ unit         <chr> "Corporate Planning", "Sales Operations", "Sales Operatio…
#> $ author       <chr> "Daniel Okoye, Head of Corporate Planning", "Priya Raman,…
#> $ report_type  <chr> "aop", "sales_flash", "sales_flash", "alert", "sales_flas…
#> $ period_start <date> 2025-01-01, 2024-12-30, 2025-01-06, 2025-01-15, 2025-01-…
#> $ period_end   <date> 2025-12-31, 2025-01-05, 2025-01-12, 2025-01-15, 2025-01-…
#> $ published    <date> 2024-12-16, 2025-01-06, 2025-01-13, 2025-01-15, 2025-01-…

title: Searching the reports with ragnar
text:
Step 2: create an empty store
embed = NULL turns off embeddings. extra_cols declares the metadata columns that every chunk will carry, with their types. Passing zero rows of the reports table declares exactly the columns and types above.

store_path <- tempfile(fileext = ".duckdb")

meta_cols <- c(
  "id",
  "title",
  "unit",
  "author",
  "report_type",
  "period_start",
  "period_end",
  "published"
)
report_store <- ragnar::ragnar_store_create(
  store_path,
  embed = NULL,
  extra_cols = reports[0, meta_cols]
)

Use a real path such as "reports.duckdb" instead of tempfile() to keep the store between sessions.

title: Searching the reports with ragnar
section: Step 3: chunk one report and attach its metadata
text:
Step 3: chunk one report and attach its metadata
ragnar splits a document into overlapping chunks of about 1,600 characters. Each chunk records where it starts and ends in the body, and the headings above it (context). Chunk the body text, and set origin to the report id so every chunk links back to its report.

report <- reports |>
  dplyr::filter(id == "ecommerce-2025-06")

chunks <-
  report$body |>
  ragnar::MarkdownDocument(origin = report$id) |>
  ragnar::markdown_chunk()

To browse the chunks with each one rendered as Markdown, open ragnar’s viewer. It is a Shiny app, so run it in your own session:

chunks |>
  ragnar::ragnar_chunks_view()

The chunks know nothing about the report yet. Pulling in the metadata is one mutate(): every metadata value is a single value, so it is repeated on each chunk.

chunks <-
  chunks |>
  cross_join(report |> select(-body))

chunks |>
  dplyr::select(start, end, id, unit, report_type, published)
#> # @document@origin: ecommerce-2025-06
#> # A tibble:         4 × 6
#>   start   end id                unit             report_type published 
#>   <int> <int> <chr>             <chr>            <chr>       <date>    
#> 1     1  1603 ecommerce-2025-06 Digital Commerce ecommerce   2025-07-04
#> 2   772  2343 ecommerce-2025-06 Digital Commerce ecommerce   2025-07-04
#> 3  1604  3212 ecommerce-2025-06 Digital Commerce ecommerce   2025-07-04
#> 4  2344  3908 ecommerce-2025-06 Digital Commerce ecommerce   2025-07-04

title: Searching the reports with ragnar
Searching the reports with ragnar
text:
Step 5: build the search index
This builds the ‘DuckDB’ full-text (BM25) index over the chunk text and headings. Run it after every insert.

ragnar::ragnar_store_build_index(report_store)

Check the result: every report has chunks and no metadata is missing.

DBI::dbGetQuery(
  report_store@con,
  "
  select count(distinct id) as reports,
         count(*) as n
  from chunks"
)
#>   reports   n
#> 1     118 396

title: Searching the reports with ragnar
text:
Step 6: search
ragnar_retrieve_bm25() returns one row per matching chunk, with all of the metadata columns attached.

hits <- ragnar::ragnar_retrieve_bm25(
  report_store,
  "ShopSphere marketplace",
  top_k = 5
)

hits |>
  dplyr::select(id, unit, published, chunk_id, metric_value)
#> # A tibble: 5 × 5
#>   id                   unit                     published  chunk_id metric_value
#>   <chr>                <chr>                    <date>        <int>        <dbl>
#> 1 aop-2025             Corporate Planning       2024-12-16        1         1.87
#> 2 aop-2025             Corporate Planning       2024-12-16        2         1.84
#> 3 ecommerce-2025-01    Digital Commerce         2025-02-04        8         1.81
#> 4 pricing-2025-01      Pricing & Promotions Co… 2025-01-29      125         1.79
#> 5 sales-flash-2025-w02 Sales Operations         2025-01-13      218         1.76

How to read a row:







Column
Meaning




text
The excerpt itself, about 1,600 characters


id, title, unit, author, report_type
Which report it came from


period_start, period_end
The period the report covers


published
When the report was released


chunk_id, start, end
Which excerpt of the report, and where it sits in the body


context
The headings above the excerpt


metric_value
BM25 score. Higher is a better match. Only comparable within one search



Chunks overlap by about half, so two neighbouring chunks of the same report can both appear. Treat them as one source.

title: Searching the reports with ragnar
section: Step 7: use the store from an LLM

title: Searching the reports with ragnar
section: Use the reports from an assistant

title: Searching the reports with ragnar
text:
Conclusion

Chunk each report’s body, and attach all of its metadata to every chunk with one mutate(). Declare the metadata columns up front with extra_cols = reports[0, meta_cols].
From exported files, yaml12::read_yaml() gives the metadata and body together; convert the dates back to Date.
embed = NULL gives a BM25-only store with no embedding model.
Search with ragnar_retrieve_bm25(). Use conjunctive = TRUE to know when nothing really matched, and filter to restrict by date, unit or type.
Use SQL on the chunks table for questions about dates and counts.
When an LLM uses the store, give it a search tool that enforces as_of.
